What is a reversible change?
questions.a: A change that can be undone, bringing back the original state - melting ice to water and freezing it back.

questions.q: Give two examples of reversible changes.
questions.a: Melting of ice and stretching of a rubber band (also folding paper).

questions.q: Why is inflating a balloon reversible but bursting it not?
questions.a: Deflating restores the balloon; a burst balloon's original state cannot return.

questions.q: What is an irreversible change?
questions.a: A change that cannot be undone to get the original material back - burning paper, cooking an egg.

questions.q: Give two examples of irreversible changes.
questions.a: Burning of paper and souring of milk (also growth of a plant).

questions.q: How is cutting of paper different from burning it?
questions.a: Cutting is a reversible physical change (pieces can be rejoined); burning makes ash - irreversible.

questions.q: What happens to a metal rod on heating?
questions.a: It expands - becomes a little longer and thicker (thermal expansion).

questions.q: Give one everyday example of expansion by heat.
questions.a: Railway gaps, or a jam jar lid loosened under hot water.

questions.q: Why are gaps left between railway tracks?
questions.a: In summer the rails expand; gaps prevent bending of the track.

questions.q: What happens to a substance on cooling?
Give one example of contraction on cooling.
questions.a: A metal ring tightening on a wooden wheel when cooled, or a lid tightening in the fridge.

questions.q: Do all materials contract equally on cooling?
questions.a: No - the amount differs from material to material.
